meta.reviewer: Claude (Opus 5) via Claude Code weekly review
meta.coverage: Core tier, top 15 by priority score, plus sticky act/accumulate holdovers, plus AMKR added by operator request (19 names)
meta.disclaimer: Second-opinion research notes on @aleabitoreddit's ideas. Personal research tool — not investment advice.

focus.headline: Memory repriced. The market sold the news.
focus.dek: Server DRAM up 13–18% next quarter with Samsung asking 20%, MU's 16 LTAs and SNDK's Meta deal lock the demand in — and memory names sold off anyway. SNDK joins the book.

verdicts.view: The seats found what the posts could not. Q1 net sales were SEK 61.9m, DOWN 22% year on year, and the $799m he quotes is an opportunity pipeline, not backlog. The POET wording upgrade he read as material still resolves, in the only citable partnership language, to 'production readiness by end of 2026' — a milestone, not an order. He is not talking his book dishonestly; he is compounding forward-looking wording into a position while the reported revenue shrinks. Down 56% in a month, the market has already voted.
verdicts.execution: Stop adding. Existing tranches from the crash-week plan stand — this is a pause on new size, not a trim. The 27 August Q2 interim is the first datapoint that can test the ramp; nothing between now and then is evidence. Re-open the accumulate case only on that print.
verdicts.changesMind: Q2 interim on 27 Aug showing net sales back in growth, or a named volume order (customer, units, ASP) from Sivers or POET rather than a readiness milestone.

verdicts.view: The one name where outside research confirmed him outright. The FQ3 call puts revenue at a record $808m, up 90%, with the supply-demand gap above 30% in EMLs and pump lasers and the Japan fab fully allocated. Caveat worth holding: the shortage evidence is the CEO's own remarks, so quoting Hurlston back is not independent corroboration. The AXT deal is the harder evidence — Lumentum is prepaying $87m to reserve InP substrate through 2031, which is what a genuinely constrained buyer does.
verdicts.execution: Unchanged: the lower-beta anchor of the photonics book. Down 14% on the week with revenue accelerating is the entry the plan wants — take a tranche here rather than waiting for a bottom that is not callable.
verdicts.changesMind: The supply gap narrowing in company disclosure, or an FQ4 guide that shows the record revenue was a pull-forward rather than a run-rate.

verdicts.view: FQ1 data center revenue of $75.2bn, up 92%, with networking near tripling — the demand hub is not the question. The question this week is who pays. NVIDIA returned roughly $20bn to shareholders and authorised $80bn more of buyback while its customers raised capex, and Meta missed EPS badly funding that same capex. At 74.9% gross margin NVIDIA is its customers' cost line, and the first strain always shows in the payer's earnings.
verdicts.execution: Unchanged: express the view through the suppliers this map surfaces rather than through NVDA itself. Hold as a separate core-portfolio decision, not a desk position.
verdicts.changesMind: A hyperscaler explicitly cutting compute orders rather than capex dollars, or NVIDIA gross margin compressing below the low 70s.

verdicts.view: The number the whole bull case rests on does not survive contact with the filing. He anchors on $471m/month from H2 2027, about $5.6bn annualised; the company guides Q2 2026 to $180-198m and FY2026 to roughly $1.1bn. That is a five-fold gap between his model and management's own guide, and he presents it as the company's estimate. The '1x forward revenue' cheapness is also doing less work than it looks: Q2 is guided to non-GAAP EPS between -$0.03 and +$0.03. Record revenue that earns nothing.
verdicts.execution: Stop the scale-in. The reserved half stays reserved and existing tranches stand. Reopen only on an earnings print that puts the 2027 exit rate on a path management will underwrite in its own guidance.
verdicts.changesMind: AAOI guiding to a quarterly revenue rate consistent with $471m/month, or a named CPO customer with committed volume and positive gross-margin economics attached.

verdicts.view: Enters the roster on score, and the timing is awkward: Q2 results land 4 August, one day out, against a guide already embedding 46% growth. The desk's interest in AMD is CPO adoption, and that claim rests entirely on channel checks and a Rosenblatt note — no AMD disclosure. Helios and MI450 ship in H2 2026 on pluggable optics, with co-packaged optics described as a future-generation option, which puts any AAOI or Sivers read-through in 2027 at the earliest. The accelerator business meanwhile compounds independently of the photonics narrative.
verdicts.execution: No action into tomorrow's print — that is a coin-flip on execution, not on the thesis. If you want AMD, the entry decision belongs after the guide, and it is a whole-company accelerator call rather than a CPO derivative.
verdicts.changesMind: AMD committing to CPO in a product disclosure with a named generation and date, which would convert the SIVE/AAOI read-through from inference into schedule.

verdicts.view: The strongest of the four capex payers and the only one whose spend is visibly funded by an accelerating business: Q2 revenue $119.8bn up 24%, Cloud $24.8bn up 82%, record $44.9bn quarterly capex, full-year guide raised to $195-205bn. One correction to how the desk reads these numbers: roughly 60% goes to servers and only 40% to data centers and networking, so headline capex overstates the pull for the optics names. Note also it is up 12% on the week while the suppliers it funds fell — the read-through is not symmetric.
verdicts.execution: Accumulate-on-weakness hyperscaler leg, but not here — it has just rallied 12% in a week. Wait for the capex-driven derating the print already caused once; that is where the entry is.
verdicts.changesMind: Cloud growth decelerating below the 40s while capex guidance holds — spend without the revenue behind it is a different company.

verdicts.view: His recap carried Meta's capex number and dropped the earnings. Q2 EPS was $6.18 against roughly $7.14 expected, on $60.8bn revenue and $31.1bn of quarterly capex, and the stock fell about 8%. This is the bias to name: a supply-chain analyst reads hyperscaler capex as a demand signal and stops reading there, but the same line that funds the suppliers is what missed at the payer. Part of the capex raise is memory cost inflation, not incremental compute units, so the dollars overstate unit demand too.
verdicts.execution: Step off accumulate. The supplier read-through is intact; the equity is being derated for the spending that creates it. Holding Meta and holding Meta's suppliers are now opposite expressions of the same view, so pick one — the desk already owns the supply side.
verdicts.changesMind: Free cash flow stabilising with capex held flat, or the compute-leasing revenue line becoming large enough to show up in segment disclosure.

verdicts.view: Enters on score, but almost every mention is by association — the AXT long-term agreement, the Morgan Stanley CPO-visibility trio alongside LITE and SIVE, the Hurlston shortage post. There is no dedicated Coherent thesis in this corpus with numbers attached, which matters because Coherent is the one photonics prime whose datacom exposure sits inside a much larger, slower industrial business. Down 33% on the month with the same shortage tailwind as Lumentum.
verdicts.execution: No dedicated action. LITE already carries the InP-shortage exposure at higher purity and with the numbers disclosed. If Coherent is to earn a position it needs its own datacom segment math, not the sector's.
verdicts.changesMind: A dedicated post or company disclosure sizing the datacom/CPO segment separately, which would make the conglomerate discount an opportunity rather than a reason to own LITE instead.

verdicts.view: Down 25% on the week and 41% on the month, and the week's coverage was about the sell-off's framing rather than the business — he pushed back on media treating Leopold's multi-year thesis as a collapse. That is a fair objection but it is sentiment analysis, not evidence. The memory evidence that did arrive is Micron's: record DRAM revenue at 84.9% gross margin, which reads as a cycle peak. SNDK is NAND-levered rather than DRAM-levered, so the peak-margin warning is adjacent, not direct.
verdicts.execution: Starter tranche from the 16 July call stands; hold it. Do not add into a 41% monthly drawdown on sentiment arguments alone — the next add wants a NAND-specific pricing or contract datapoint.
verdicts.changesMind: NAND contract pricing rolling over, or the DRAM margin peak spilling into NAND in the next round of supplier guidance.

verdicts.view: Enters on mention volume, and the mentions are structural rather than thesis-driven: the Amkor ten-year packaging partnership, the Innolight silicon-photonics estimate revisions, FormFactor's CPO revenue commentary. TSMC is how this map's whole supply side gets built, which makes it the least differentiated way to own the theme — every edge the desk has found is in the small suppliers upstream of it.
verdicts.execution: No desk action. Treat as a core-portfolio holding decision if you want it, not a position this research produces an edge on.
verdicts.changesMind: A capacity or pricing disclosure specific to advanced packaging or silicon photonics that the small-cap suppliers cannot express.

verdicts.view: The wording change he flagged — 'production' replacing 'production readiness' for Sivers lasers by end-2026 — is the week's most-cited photonics claim and I could not verify it. The only citable partnership language remains readiness by end of 2026 with customer prototypes in H1. He also notes POET fell to roughly $800m cash against a $1.2bn market cap, which is a real floor argument. Credibility scaffolding intact, economics still absent.
verdicts.execution: Unchanged: speculative sizing only. Trigger remains a named customer or actual production revenue, not a press-release verb change.
verdicts.changesMind: A purchase order or revenue-recognising shipment for the optical interposer, which would convert the Sivers link from a shared narrative into shared revenue.

verdicts.view: The CHIPS award is confirmed: a $300m letter of intent for silicon photonics and co-packaged optics R&D, with Commerce taking roughly 1% equity, and AMD, Broadcom, Meta, Microsoft and NVIDIA named as SCALE CPO customers. His read-through to SIVE and LITE is directionally right — this is federal money aimed squarely at the desk's theme. His puzzlement that GFS stayed down is the weaker part: $300m is immaterial to a $27bn company, and the market priced it that way correctly.
verdicts.execution: No dedicated action — the SIVE and LITE positions already carry the CPO-platform exposure with more torque. GFS is the confirmation, not the vehicle.
verdicts.changesMind: GlobalFoundries disclosing silicon-photonics revenue as a segment, which would make it a CPO pure-play rather than a diversified foundry with a grant.

verdicts.view: The operating story is intact — up to 1.2GW secured in Pennsylvania, more than 3GW contracted by year-end, and for a neocloud energised capacity is the binding constraint. The financing story is the problem. Q1 revenue was $399m, annualising near $1.6bn against a $3-3.4bn full-year target, so almost the entire guide sits in the second half, and capex plans run an order of magnitude above revenue. This is a funding-terms equity before it is a compute equity, and Q2 lands 12 August.
verdicts.execution: Step off accumulate until the 12 August print. Hold what exists. The thing to underwrite before adding is the next raise's terms, not GPU demand.
verdicts.changesMind: Q2 showing the H2 revenue step-up on schedule, or capacity funded without dilutive equity — either turns this back into an operating story.

verdicts.view: Q2 was the strongest revenue growth in over fifteen years — $16.1bn, up 25% — and still a GAAP loss of $2.16 a share against non-GAAP $0.42. Q3 is guided above consensus. The desk's actual interest is the China CPU long-term agreement story, which is a Reuters report and appears nowhere in the release; the foundry milestones everyone quotes come from call commentary I could not tie to a filing. On the disclosed schedule 14A is risk production in 2027 and high volume in 2028, so external foundry revenue is not a 2026 or 2027 event.
verdicts.execution: No action on this corpus. Any Intel position is a whole-company turnaround judgment on a multi-year clock, not a read-through from this map's photonics theme.
verdicts.changesMind: A named external 14A customer with committed volume, or GAAP profitability arriving before the 2028 ramp.

verdicts.view: Enters on score off one substantive datapoint and several breadth lists: the ARR target revised to $4bn-plus on new AI cloud contracts, with Microsoft, NVIDIA, Perplexity and Figure named as customers. That is a real upgrade in counterparty quality for a converted bitcoin miner. The rest of the week's mentions are drawdown-and-snapback lists, which inflate the mention count without adding evidence. Same structural question as NBIS: contracted ARR is not funded capacity.
verdicts.execution: No action. NBIS already carries the neocloud exposure and has more disclosure behind it. If the neocloud leg is to be doubled, that is a sizing decision, not a second name.
verdicts.changesMind: ARR converting to reported revenue on schedule with the capex funded, which would make IREN a genuine alternative to NBIS rather than a correlated duplicate.

verdicts.view: Quiet again — three mentions, all as a named partner in the Sivers capacity-ramp web rather than a dedicated thesis. The position's logic is unchanged and deliberately boring: JBL is the profitable, diversified way to hold the 1.6T and CPO build without underwriting a single small-cap's ramp. In a week where the pure-plays fell 25-56% and JBL fell 2%, that is the leg doing exactly its job.
verdicts.execution: Starter position stands. Its function is ballast against the photonics book's beta, so it does not need a catalyst to justify holding.
verdicts.changesMind: Losing the photonics-adjacent programmes, or the diversification thesis breaking down in a quarter where datacom growth stops offsetting the legacy segments.

verdicts.view: The cleanest datapoint of the week for the whole map: capex raised to $220bn from $200bn, AWS up 37% at its fastest in eighteen quarters, and Jassy saying explicitly that even $220bn will not meet 2026 demand, with the same true in 2027. Worth naming that part of the raise is memory cost inflation rather than more units — a point that cuts against reading the number as pure supplier demand. Up 16% on the week, so the market agrees.
verdicts.execution: Core-position logic, dollar-cost average — unchanged. Do not chase a 16% weekly move; the averaging schedule is the discipline that handles this.
verdicts.changesMind: AWS growth decelerating while capex holds, or capacity catching up with demand — Jassy's own framing is the falsifier here.

verdicts.view: The earnings transcript delivered the confirmation the thesis wanted in the company's own words — progress in co-packaged optics, plus the 800V transition supporting SiC and GaN demand. Two independent legs, a specialty-foundry value floor and a free photonics option, and the CPO leg is now management-stated rather than inferred. Down 14% on the week with the print in hand.
verdicts.execution: The value leg justifies a real starter position and the photonics leg is the free upside; the weekly drawdown is an adding window, not a warning. Size in euros and accept the European liquidity.
verdicts.changesMind: The CPO progress language disappearing from the next transcript, or the SiC/800V ramp slipping — the value floor alone does not carry the position.

verdicts.view: Added to coverage at the operator's request, outside the top-15 rule — AMKR ranks 40th on score with three mentions. The analyst bought it in the $40s and called the post-earnings drop surprising given the NVDA $1.5B deal and the TSM ten-year agreement. He is right that the reaction was severe and right about why: his own 29 July note observes markets are rewarding existing acceleration over growth a year out, and names AMKR as the example. What separates this from SIVE or AAOI is that the numbers here are reported rather than modelled — Amkor posted record Q2 net sales of $1.90bn, up 26%, with $0.70 of diluted EPS. The catch is that the record quarter was led by Computing and Automotive & Industrial, not by the AI packaging ramp, and he concedes the name is a 2028 story with partial 2027 ramps.
verdicts.execution: Scale in slowly and size it as a multi-year hold, not a catalyst trade — the AI revenue is two years out and the drawdown can continue without anything being wrong. Quarterly tranches rather than a single entry, and no adding on headlines about the NVDA agreement: that money is a prepayment for capacity, so it appears in the cash flow long before it appears in earnings.
verdicts.changesMind: The Arizona and advanced-packaging capacity expansion slipping past 2028, or a quarter where Computing revenue rolls over before the AI ramp arrives to replace it — that would leave the name carrying cyclical OSAT risk with none of the AI upside yet in the numbers.
